summary: Implement a doubly linked list with get, addAtHead, addAtTail, addAtIndex and deleteAtIndex.
mainInsight: Use a doubly linked list with sentinel head and tail nodes plus a size counter: sentinels eliminate empty-list and boundary special cases, and the size lets you walk from whichever end is closer to the index.

approaches.name: Doubly linked with sentinels
approaches.summary: prev/next pointers, dummy head and tail, size counter.
approaches.timeComplexity: O(1) at ends, O(min(i, n-i)) by index

personalSolution.approach: Doubly linked list with sentinels and size
personalSolution.notes: Good design: sentinels plus walking from the nearer end.

promptVariants: What simplifies insertion/deletion at the list boundaries?
Why use dummy head and tail nodes?
options: Sentinel nodes remove special cases for empty lists and ends
They make indexing O(1) because positions are stored in the sentinels
They sort the list so insertion points are always found quickly
They save memory because the real nodes need no next pointers
cards.answer: Sentinel nodes remove special cases for empty lists and ends
cards.explanation: Every real node always has a prev and next, so the same pointer-update code works everywhere.

promptVariants: Why do you walk from the tail when the index is in the second half?
What does the size counter enable?
cards.answer: With prev pointers you can traverse backwards from the tail, so any index is reachable in at most about size/2 steps (O(min(i, n - i)) instead of O(i)). The size field tells you which end is closer and validates indices in O(1).
cards.explanation: Constant factor improvement, same worst-case O(n).

promptVariants: Complete the statement: Time of addAtHead / addAtTail: ___
cards.explanation: Sentinels give direct access to both ends.

promptVariants: What is the space cost and what do prev pointers add?
What does a doubly linked list cost in memory compared with a singly linked list?
cards.answer: O(n) nodes (plus two sentinels); each node stores an extra prev pointer compared with a singly linked list.
cards.explanation: Trade extra memory for bidirectional traversal.

promptVariants: In addAtIndex, why does the step count differ between walking from the head and from the tail?
cards.code:
curr = self.head
steps = index
if not is_close_to_head:
    curr = self.tail
    steps = self.size - index + 1
for _ in range(steps):
    curr = curr.next if is_close_to_head else curr.prev
new_node = Node(val)
next_node = curr.next
cards.answer: We want curr to be the node BEFORE the insertion position (the predecessor of index). From the head sentinel (position -1) that is `index` steps; from the tail sentinel (position size) it is size - index + 1 steps backwards. Then new_node is linked between curr and curr.next.
keyPoints: curr = predecessor of the target index
cards.explanation: Off-by-one errors are the main risk.

promptVariants: What should addAtIndex(index == size, val) do and addAtIndex(index > size, val)?
options: index == size appends at the end; index > size does nothing
Both append to the end, regardless of how large the index is
Both raise errors because the index must be strictly below the size
index == size does nothing; index > size appends at the end
cards.answer: index == size appends at the end; index > size does nothing
cards.explanation: The specification allows insertion at the end but ignores larger indices.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Both append to the end, regardless of ho: Indices beyond size are invalid and ignored.
